headline: Challenger is seeing its strongest growth in CPI-linked guaranteed lifetime income products as retirees seek inflation protection within their income portfolios.
reasoning: Mandy Mannix notes that Challenger's fastest-growing retirement income products are those with CPI linkage, as retirees want certainty that their income will keep pace with rising prices. The appeal is simple: once a CPI-linked annuity is in place, the retiree does not need to worry about inflation eroding their income. This reflects a broader structural shift in how retirees want to manage longevity and inflation risk simultaneously, favouring guaranteed income solutions over purely accumulation-based drawdown strategies.
quote: Again, if I just take a slight challenger plug here, that's why I believe the strongest growth of our, um, guaranteed lifetime income solutions have been those that have been CPI linked because people just know, okay, well, they just don't have to worry about that. Then if I've got some CPI linkage in my in my retirement.

headline: Cost of living is the single biggest persistent challenge for Australian retirees, and the lack of salary growth means inflation erodes fixed retirement savings faster than working-age Australians realise.
reasoning: Mandy Mannix explains that retirees, unlike workers, no longer have the implicit hedge of wage growth keeping pace with inflation. Once retired, individuals must convert a lump sum into an income stream that sustains purchasing power over time. Even before recent elevated inflation and geopolitical risks, cost of living ranked as the top concern in Challenger's Happiness Index research (2,000 Australians aged 60+, conducted with YouGov in February, run three years in a row). The structural mismatch between a fixed or self-managed income pool and rising prices is, in her view, the defining financial challenge of retirement.
quote: Yeah, it's the biggest challenge, um, retirees and retirees face through. If we look at the research we did most recently, which was the Happiness Index, 2000, um, Australians 60 years and over, done in, in combination with YouGov in February this year. And we've done it three years in a row, cost of living every year. So even before this year, where you had more talk about inflation and geopolitical risks and, um, spikes in the oil price and the like, this is constantly an issue. And the reason I think it's an issue is really simple. It's that, you know, when you retire, you're no longer getting an income. You no longer have a have this sort of thought in the back of your mind that your income will probably increase with inflation. You suddenly have this pot of money that you that you have to try and turn into some sort of income. That's going to mean that you can continue to to buy a bottle of milk, even though, you know, it might have been $1.50 last week, you know, last year, and it's $2 this year.

headline: Challenger's Mandy Mannix warns low financial literacy and longevity risk are creating a retirement income crisis as 250,000 Australians retire annually
reasoning: Mannix argues that limited financial literacy causes retirees to do nothing with their savings, leading to under-spending and large residual estates at death. She notes that 1 in 3 Australians will live past 90 and suggests 30 years is the new average retirement duration, creating significant longevity risk. The psychological shift from accumulation to decumulation is described as a massive challenge that the industry, super funds, advisors and government all need to address. She emphasises that retirees who have had financial guidance tend to have more confident and happier retirements, but there are not enough advisors to meet demand. Behavioral bias and information overload are cited as key reasons financial literacy remains a persistent gap.
quote: One of the biggest challenges we find is this limited financial literacy. And when people don't understand something, they then tend to do nothing. And so, you know, when you hear all of these discussions around fear of running out or people not spending and, and actually dying with quite a lot of their spending or their assets left, a lot of that is because they don't really have confidence to spend. And that confidence comes from financial literacy. We also know that, you know, when people have a plan or they've had financial guidance from an advisor, for example, that they do tend to have a great deal more confidence and have happier and more confident retirements, but there's not enough advisors to go around.

headline: Challenger launches Institute for Lifetime Income to build evidence-based research platform and improve retirement income literacy across the industry
reasoning: Mannix explains that Challenger has accumulated decades of proprietary research, white papers and policy engagement on retirement income but has kept it internal. The Institute for Lifetime Income is designed to make that knowledge public and serve as an open platform bringing together industry experts and evidence-based research. The initiative is timed to coincide with a demographic inflection point where 250,000 Australians retire each year. The goal is to reduce retiree anxiety, improve confidence to spend, and help convert accumulated nest eggs into sustainable income streams.
quote: We're doing this because challenger has been a leader in retirement income for decades. And over those decades, we've written a lot of research, um, really engaged with both our, our own clients, but also other retirees and retirees in the market. We've written a number of white papers. We've been engaged in policy. Um, so that's been over several decades, but that information has all been kept inside. What we want to do now is bring that out so that it can be a real platform to continue to promote that, um, you know, improving and understanding of retirement income. We want to use it to bring together more evidence based research, but also bring in insights and conversations, not just with our own experts, but with all of the industry experts as we're seeing, you know, more and more as this wonderful, um, system of ours grows.

headline: Inflation is the primary financial threat for Australian retirees, eroding purchasing power in ways that wage earners are shielded from
reasoning: Aaron Minney notes that retirees face a structural disadvantage relative to workers when it comes to inflation, because they lack any automatic cost-of-living adjustment to their income. Prices rise and never come back down, meaning that living off savings becomes progressively harder over time. The Reserve Bank has flagged inflation as the number one concern across the population, and Challenger's own research found two in three retirees are worried about cost of living. The psychological impact is significant — high inflation causes retirees to withdraw from spending, denting confidence and reducing quality of life. The challenge is not just meeting bills today but ensuring money lasts five to ten years into the future.
quote: As we saw last week, the reserve Bank highlighted that inflation is the number one concern across the population. You know, when we spoke to retirees earlier this year, 2 in 3 are worried about the cost of living. And one of the big reasons for that is they don't have any way of automatically adjusting for it. Like when you're working, most of the time you've got a wage or something that keeps up with it. But when you're in retirement, each time there's inflation, that price level just goes up and up again. So it's a bit harder to sort of adjust for, you know, we always think about inflation going up and down. But inflation goes up. Up never comes down. Prices go up. Yeah. But they don't come down. And so when you're living off your savings as you do in retirement, that's a challenge that makes the whole concept of keeping your money lasting through retirement. That's step harder for retirees.

headline: Inflation-linked lifetime income streams are gaining traction as a retirement solution, with Challenger seeing strong retiree interest in products that provide a guaranteed cost-of-living-adjusted income floor
reasoning: Minney highlights that innovations in lifetime income streams — offered by large super funds and retail platforms — now incorporate inflation protection and are seeing increasing uptake from inflation-worried retirees. The age pension provides a built-in inflation adjustment but is insufficient on its own for those with any meaningful assets. Lifetime income streams can cover the baseline income need without requiring retirees to commit all their capital, giving them confidence that essential expenses are covered regardless of how long they live. The government's best practice retirement income principles have further legitimised this product category, and newer versions are market-linked, allowing retirees to remain invested while still having longevity protection.
quote: You can have an inflation linked income stream. You know we've seen a lot of innovations now sort of big super fans, some of the retail platforms with their lifetime income streams and some of those have inflation protection in there. And we're seeing a lot of interest in that from retirees that are worried about the cost of living. And the good thing is you don't need to put everything into it. It's a little bit of that. We'll cover that baseline. And that's what people are after... We're now seeing this increase in lifetime income streams. So this is part of the government's best practice principles. They've highlighted that this is money that will last for life. You know, and we're seeing innovations in those that are linked to markets. So you can keep them invested.

headline: Australian equity dividends have risen only 18% over ten years versus a 35% rise in cost of living, creating a false sense of inflation protection for retirees relying on dividend income
reasoning: Minney cautions that equities and dividends provide a false sense of security for retirees seeking inflation protection. While equities generate strong real returns during the accumulation phase, what matters in retirement is the income stream. Looking back ten years, Australian dividends have grown 18% while the cost of living has risen 35%, meaning retirees relying solely on dividends have had to eat into capital. Dividends can grow over time and will outpace low inflation (around 2%), but they do not adjust quickly enough when there is an inflation shock, making them an incomplete solution on their own.
quote: If you go back ten years and look at someone who's living off dividends from from their equities in Australia, dividends have gone up 18%. But if you look at what's happened to the cost of living over that time, it's gone up 35%. So that dividend stream you're getting, the dollars haven't gone up as much. So this is where you need to sort of eat into a bit of the capital. And that's what raises them are concerns... The challenge is, is whether the dividend keeps up with the inflation, you know, and when inflation was sort of 2% or so, it was growth and dividends were keeping up with that when there was this shock. The dividends haven't adjusted quickly enough.

headline: Challenger's Aaron Minney outlines the role of lifetime income streams in inflation-proofing retirement portfolios
reasoning: Aaron Minney highlights that retirees now have access to three types of retirement income options: lump sum, flexible account-based pensions, and lifetime income streams. He notes growing adoption of lifetime income streams, driven by government best-practice principles requiring income to last for life. These products can be linked to markets for growth exposure or structured as guaranteed income, either fixed or CPI-linked, to protect against inflation. He emphasises that it is never too late to rebalance a retirement strategy to account for inflation.
quote: And one of the things we're seeing now with the funds is got access to sort of three different types of retirement options. One's your lump sum. Yeah. So you can always been able to do access to money as you need it. The other one is the flexible income stream. You know the account based pension that people have been used to keeps the money. Investor keeps it there and available. Yeah. But we're now seeing this increase in lifetime income streams. So this is part of the government's best practice principles. They've highlighted that this is money that will last for life. You know, and we're seeing innovations in those that are linked to markets. So you can keep them invested in shares and keep that growing over time. Or you can have them that are more secure and guaranteed, either fixed or linked to, you know, CPI inflation, for example, so that you know that income there will always keep up with inflation.

headline: Elevated oil prices likely to persist as Middle East conflict drives prices back to ~$84/barrel with futures curve signalling no expected resolution
reasoning: Kearns notes oil jumped almost 9% last week and has risen further after weekend strikes, returning to around $84 a barrel from the pre-war ~$70 level. The futures curve is remarkably flat, indicating markets do not expect a swift resolution and a return of full oil supply from the Middle East. He views this as an appropriate market assessment given ongoing uncertainty.
quote: Last week we had an almost 9% increase in the oil price. It's jumped again the beginning of this week after the weekend. Um more strikes pushing the price higher. So you know, we're back around $84 a barrel having got back around to sort of the $70 pre-war levels. Uh, that's that's fairly significant. And if you look at the futures curve, it's actually remarkably flat. Um, so, you know, markets aren't expecting a resolution with the oil price coming back down. And so, you know, I think we are in a situation where we might go back and forth, back and forth some resolution.

headline: Over 200 economists including 15 Nobel laureates urge policy action on AI-linked labour disruption risk, warning social safety nets may be inadequate if large-scale job losses materialise
reasoning: Kearns describes a short letter signed by over 200 economists, including 15 Nobel laureates, urging governments to act on AI even among signatories who remain sceptical about AI's ultimate impact. The core concern is that AI could cause large-scale job losses and labour market disruption in a tail-risk scenario. Policymakers need to assess whether taxation systems can raise enough revenue to fund unemployment benefits and whether social safety nets are adequate. Kearns frames this as not the most likely outcome but a plausible one given the pace of AI development and statements from industry leaders.
quote: So we had a very short letter. It was only 88 words, I think, released by over 200 economists and more were signing it. I think there are 15 Nobel laureates who signed it. And essentially they're saying we just need to act on AI. So, you know, even some economists, notable economists who've been skeptical about AI and remain skeptical about AI, are still urging action. And what what they're essentially saying is there is some chance that AI is completely disruptive to our economy and leads to large scale job losses. To insure against that, we need to make sure that we've got mechanisms to protect people, you know, so do we have our, you know, our taxation system? Is it going to be able to raise enough revenue to be able to fund enough unemployment benefits, how are we going to deal with there being a large amount of unemployed people? So this is a not the most likely case, but it's certainly possible if some of what is, you know, how rapidly we're seeing AI develop and what the leaders in the AI industry say is possible. Out of that, we could have pretty wide disruptions of the labor market.

headline: RBA deliberately slowing Australian economy to tame domestically-generated inflation, with higher unemployment and slower living standards growth an expected consequence
reasoning: Kearns explains that Australian inflation is not purely imported via oil prices but reflects domestic demand running too hot relative to supply capacity. The RBA is deliberately trying to slow the economy, which will result in higher unemployment and slower growth in living standards. Consumers are picking up on this dynamic, which contributes to the negative sentiment readings.
quote: The inflation we've been seeing in Australia is not just because of the Middle East conflict and higher oil prices. It's actually been because demand in the Australian economy is too strong for what we're able to supply. So the reserve Bank has been trying to slow the economy. You know, we do need to accept that that's going to result in a bit of a higher unemployment rate, slower growth in our standards of living. You know, and consumers do pick up on that. And that that is part of the negative sentiment.

headline: Challenger economist warns AI-linked labour disruption is a tail risk requiring policy preparation, even if not the base case
reasoning: Jonathan Kearns argues that while large-scale AI-driven job losses are not the most likely outcome, the probability is non-trivial and warrants policy action now. He draws an analogy to home insurance: you don't expect your house to burn down, but you prepare for the possibility. He notes that even Sam Altman has acknowledged AI disruption has progressed more slowly than expected in terms of labour market impact. Key policy questions include whether tax systems can raise enough revenue to fund unemployment benefits if displacement accelerates. The fact that economists embedded inside leading AI firms (OpenAI, Anthropic) have signed warnings adds weight to the concern.
quote: You know, these are the lot of the people who've signed it are researching in AI or actually working in some of the the AI firms. So the chief economist at OpenAI, the chief economist at anthropic, has signed it. So they're in the weeds now... there is still this risk. And so, you know, it's like saying you don't expect your house to burn down, but there's some chance it will. And so you take out insurance. I think about it in the same kind of way. There is some chance that AI is as disruptive as some of the leading advocates suggest. We want to be ready for that world. And so we need to think about our our policies, right for that.
